data.title: Lichen planus — viva
data.summary: Papulosquamous & erythroderma · 30 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Lichen planus** (Papulosquamous & erythroderma)_

**Q1. Define lichen planus (LP).**
- Chronic, immune-mediated (T-cell) inflammatory disease of skin, mucous membranes, hair and nails, classically presenting as pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar (flat-topped), plane-surfaced papules and plaques — the '6 Ps' (pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar, papules, plaques)

**Q2. Aetiopathogenesis.**
- Cell-mediated cytotoxicity: CD8+ T cells target an altered basal keratinocyte antigen (presented via MHC class I) → apoptosis via perforin/granzyme, Fas–FasL; IFN-γ, TNF-α, CXCL9/10 (Th1)
- Associations: hepatitis C virus (oral LP, Mediterranean/Japan), drugs, contact allergens (amalgam — oral), vaccines (HBV), stress, autoimmune disease (thyroid, alopecia areata, vitiligo)

**Q3. Describe the clinical features.**
- Flexor wrists, forearms, shins, ankles, lower back, genitals; symmetrical; intense itch; Koebner phenomenon
- Wickham's striae: fine white lacy network on the surface (focal hypergranulosis) — better seen with oil/dermoscopy
- Heals with marked post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in Indian skin
- Mucosa: oral (50–70%) — reticular (commonest, buccal mucosa), erosive, atrophic, plaque, bullous, papular; genital — glans annular lesions; vulvo-vaginal-gingival syndrome

**Q4. Name the clinical variants.**
- Hypertrophic (shins, verrucous — risk of SCC), annular, linear (Blaschko/Koebner), atrophic, actinic (lichen planus actinicus — sun-exposed, Middle East/India), bullous LP and LP pemphigoides (anti-BP180), ulcerative (palmoplantar), follicular (lichen planopilaris), lichen planus pigmentosus, inverse, guttate, LP–lupus overlap, keratosis lichenoides chronica (Nekam's disease)

**Q5. Discuss variants of lichen planopilaris (PYQ).**
- Classic LPP: perifollicular erythema and scaling with scarring alopecia on vertex
- Frontal fibrosing alopecia (FFA): band-like recession of frontal/temporal hairline in post-menopausal women, eyebrow loss, facial papules
- Graham-Little–Piccardi–Lassueur syndrome: scarring scalp alopecia + non-scarring axillary/pubic alopecia + follicular spinous papules
- Treatment: potent/intralesional steroids, hydroxychloroquine, doxycycline, mycophenolate, cyclosporine, 5-α-reductase inhibitors (FFA), pioglitazone

**Q6. Nail changes in lichen planus (PYQ).**
- In ~10%; thinning, longitudinal ridging and splitting (onychorrhexis), dorsal pterygium (fusion of proximal nail fold to bed — characteristic, permanent), trachyonychia (twenty-nail dystrophy), anonychia, red lunulae, subungual hyperkeratosis
- Treat early to prevent permanent damage — intralesional triamcinolone, systemic steroids, retinoids

**Q7. Histopathology of LP.**
- Compact orthokeratosis (no parakeratosis), wedge-shaped hypergranulosis (Wickham's striae), irregular acanthosis with saw-tooth rete ridges, basal vacuolar degeneration with Civatte (colloid) bodies, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate hugging the dermo-epidermal junction, pigment incontinence; Max-Joseph spaces (artifactual clefts)
- DIF: shaggy fibrinogen at BMZ, IgM-positive cytoid bodies

**Q8. Define lichenoid reaction and cutaneous lichenoid tissue reaction (PYQ).**
- Lichenoid tissue reaction (interface dermatitis): basal keratinocyte damage (vacuolar change, apoptotic cells) with band-like infiltrate
- Lichenoid diseases: LP, lichenoid drug eruption, lichen nitidus, lichen striatus, LP-like keratosis, GVHD, lupus (vacuolar), EM, fixed drug, lichenoid keratosis, PLEVA, poikiloderma

**Q9. Differentiate lichenoid drug eruption from idiopathic LP.**
- Drugs: antimalarials, gold, β-blockers, ACE inhibitors, thiazides, anti-TB (isoniazid, ethambutol), NSAIDs, imatinib, checkpoint inhibitors, sildenafil
- Clinical: photodistributed, generalised, eczematous/psoriasiform, less Wickham's striae, mucosa less involved, latency weeks–months, resolves slowly after withdrawal
- Histology: parakeratosis, eosinophils, deeper perivascular infiltrate, more necrotic keratinocytes

**Q10. Differentiate LP from DLE (PYQ).**
- LP: purple, polygonal, Wickham's striae, flexures, itchy, hyperpigmentation, no follicular plugging, compact orthokeratosis, band-like infiltrate, DIF — fibrinogen and cytoid bodies
- DLE: red scaly plaques with adherent scale and follicular plugs (carpet-tack sign), face/ears/scalp, photosensitive, atrophy and scarring, depigmentation, periadnexal and perivascular superficial and deep infiltrate, mucin, thick BMZ; DIF — granular IgG/IgM/C3 at DEJ (lupus band)

**Q11. What is Nekam's disease? (PYQ)**
- Keratosis lichenoides chronica: rare chronic lichenoid dermatosis with violaceous keratotic papules in linear/reticulate arrangement on limbs and trunk, seborrhoeic-dermatitis-like facial lesions, nail and oral involvement; resistant to therapy (acitretin, PUVA)

**Q12. Oral LP — significance and management.**
- Reticular often asymptomatic; erosive painful; risk of SCC ~1% (erosive/atrophic types) — long-term follow-up and biopsy of suspicious areas
- Exclude amalgam contact allergy (patch test), HCV, drugs; good oral hygiene, avoid spicy food/tobacco
- Topical potent steroid in orabase/gel (clobetasol), tacrolimus 0.1% ointment, intralesional steroid; systemic steroids, retinoids, HCQ, dapsone, mycophenolate for severe

**Q13. Treatment of cutaneous LP.**
- Localised: potent topical steroid, intralesional triamcinolone for hypertrophic lesions, tacrolimus
- Generalised/rapidly spreading: oral prednisolone 30–60 mg tapered over 4–6 weeks, or betamethasone/dexamethasone weekly oral minipulse (OMP — popular in India), acitretin, NB-UVB/PUVA, metronidazole, griseofulvin (older), methotrexate, cyclosporine, azathioprine, mycophenolate, JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, baricitinib) for refractory
- Sedating antihistamines for itch; counsel about pigmentation

**Q14. What is lichen planus pigmentosus (LPP)?**
- Variant in darker skin (India, Middle East): slate-grey to brown macules on face, neck, flexures (inverse type) — little itch, chronic; triggers: mustard oil, amla oil, hair dye, sun
- Differential: ashy dermatosis (erythema dyschromicum perstans), melasma, Riehl's melanosis, FDE, acanthosis nigricans
- Treatment difficult: photoprotection, tacrolimus, topical steroid short, tranexamic acid, isotretinoin low-dose, Q-switched laser (caution)

**Q15. Prognosis.**
- Cutaneous LP usually remits in 1–2 years (hypertrophic and oral persist longer); recurrence ~20%; residual pigmentation lasts long

**Q16. Describe dermoscopy of LP.**
- Wickham's striae — white reticular/ radial streaks, 'white network' or 'leaf venation'; red dotted/ linear vessels at periphery; grey-blue dots (pigment incontinence) in resolving/pigmented lesions; useful to differentiate LP from psoriasis and lichenoid drug eruption

**Q17. What is hepatitis C association and its relevance in India?**
- Associations vary geographically — strong in Japan and Mediterranean, weak in India; still advisable to test HCV/HBV in erosive oral LP and extensive disease; LP may flare with interferon therapy (older HCV treatment)

**Q18. Describe genital LP and vulvovaginal-gingival syndrome.**
- Men: annular violaceous papules on glans, 'white lacy' lesions; women: erosive vulvar/vaginal LP with scarring, synechiae, introital stenosis, dyspareunia, + desquamative gingivitis (vulvovaginal-gingival syndrome) — chronic, risk of SCC; treat with clobetasol, tacrolimus, vaginal dilators

**Q19. What is lichen planus pemphigoides vs bullous LP?**
- Bullous LP: blisters within LP lesions due to intense interface damage (Max-Joseph spaces) — DIF negative
- LP pemphigoides: LP plus tense blisters on previously normal skin with antibodies to BP180 (NC16A — MCW-4 epitope); DIF linear IgG/C3 at BMZ; treat like BP + LP (steroids, dapsone, tetracyclines)

**Q20. Describe hypertrophic LP and its risks.**
- Thick hyperkeratotic verrucous plaques on shins/ankles, intensely itchy, chronic (years), pigmented; venous stasis association; may mimic or transform into SCC/keratoacanthoma (biopsy non-healing nodules)
- Treatment: intralesional/ occluded super-potent steroids, acitretin, PUVA, cryotherapy, methotrexate

**Q21. Actinic lichen planus — features.**
- Children and young adults in sunny climates (India, Middle East); annular hyperpigmented plaques with hypopigmented halo or melasma-like patches on face, neck, dorsa of hands; little itch; worse in summer; photoprotection, HCQ, topical steroids, acitretin

**Q22. LP of palms and soles — features.**
- Firm yellowish hyperkeratotic papules/ plaques, sometimes ulcerative LP of soles (painful ulcers, toenail loss — may need grafting); can mimic warts, calluses, psoriasis

**Q23. Drug-induced oral lichenoid reactions vs oral LP.**
- Oral lichenoid lesions near amalgam fillings (contact — patch test to mercury; remove amalgam), unilateral, related to drugs (antimalarials, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, antihypertensives), GVHD; oral LP is bilateral, symmetrical

**Q24. What is the Koebner phenomenon in LP?**
- Linear LP papules appear along scratch marks or trauma in ~20% of active disease (isomorphic response) — indicates active disease

**Q25. Childhood LP — differences.**
- Less common; more often linear, eruptive/generalised, actinic and hypertrophic types; oral involvement less; LP-like drug eruption and lichen nitidus overlap; treat with topical steroids, NB-UVB, oral minipulse in extensive disease

**Q26. Lichen nitidus — differentiate from LP.**
- Lichen nitidus: tiny (1–2 mm) shiny skin-coloured flat-topped papules in groups on penis, abdomen, forearms, children; Koebner; asymptomatic; histology — 'ball-and-claw' (well-circumscribed granulomatous infiltrate in a dermal papilla clasped by rete ridges); usually resolves spontaneously

**Q27. What is LP–lupus overlap?**
- Patients have features of both LP and LE (atrophic violaceous plaques on extremities, scarring); histology and DIF show mixed features; ANA may be positive; treat with antimalarials and topical steroids

**Q28. Systemic therapy of severe LP — doses.**
- Prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day for 4–6 weeks tapering, or betamethasone/dexamethasone OMP 5 mg on 2 consecutive days/week for 3–6 months
- Acitretin 25–35 mg/day for 8 weeks (strongest evidence among retinoids)
- Methotrexate 7.5–15 mg/week, metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 3–4 weeks (Indian studies), sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine (oral LP), azathioprine, MMF, cyclosporine; NB-UVB/PUVA 2–3 times weekly; JAK inhibitors for refractory

**Q29. Prognosis for scarring forms.**
- LPP, FFA and nail LP (dorsal pterygium) cause permanent scarring/ hair or nail loss — need early aggressive treatment; erosive oral and vulvar LP are chronic with malignancy risk

**Q30. What is the differential diagnosis of violaceous papules?**
- Lichen planus, lichenoid drug eruption, lichen nitidus, lichen striatus, guttate psoriasis, papular secondary syphilis, pityriasis rosea (papular), prurigo, LP-like keratosis (solitary), Kaposi sarcoma (HIV), GVHD (lichenoid)

## Quick spotter facts
- 6 Ps + Wickham's striae — LP
- Dorsal pterygium — nail LP
- Saw-tooth rete ridges, Civatte bodies, band-like infiltrate

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Lichen planus and lichenoid disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
